basis: The 6 P0 and 5 P1 distinct candidate groups in weiser-54-editorial-owner-reconciliation.v1.json. The five P1 remain provisional; P0 identities resolve to already merged canonical owners. This file adds independent source closure and editorial copy only.
method: Free public sources only. Weiser is retained as an observation locator, not independent corroboration. Web pages, diocesan and national church materials, public heritage records and museum/academic institutional sources are paraphrased. No copyrighted text reproduced.
calendar_policy: The 1962 Roman calendar supplies liturgical dates and rank. Regional domestic practice is contextual and optional; a date or season does not assert an obligation, a parish event, a priestly blessing, or a Mass rubric.

records.title_en: Las Posadas: welcoming the Holy Family
records.title_fr: Las Posadas : accueillir la Sainte Famille
records.geography: Mexico and related Latin American communities; forms vary by town, parish and diaspora.
records.occasion: Traditionally the nine evenings from 16 to 24 December. In the traditional Roman calendar this falls in Advent; it is not a universal Advent observance.
records.history: A Mexican colonial Catholic novena/procession tradition. Mexico's Ministry of Culture reports an origin tradition at Acolman in 1587 while also noting a competing account of Andalusian transmission; the exact origin is disputed.
records.meaning: The dramatic search for lodging recalls Mary and Joseph's journey and invites hospitality toward Christ and neighbour.
records.practice: Participants may walk or process with images, sing verses asking for lodging, and conclude in a host home or parish with prayer and fellowship. Household participation may include hosting or joining a local celebration.
records.contemporary: A well-attested optional regional devotion where a parish or community actually observes it. Do not imply all nine nights are required or that it is part of the 1962 Mass.
records.liturgical_class: Regional Advent devotion; neither universal liturgical observance nor obligation.
records.owner_reference: ADVT-003; do not add another canonical record or automatic Calendar event. Existing Calendar seasonal link owns discoverability.

sources.name: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, Advent December 16
sources.supports: An episcopal-catechetical account of Las Posadas around 16–24 December and the Holy Family lodging theme.
sources.limit: Describes a regional community custom, not universal Roman-rite use.

sources.name: Secretaría de Cultura de México, ¿Y tú, cómo celebras las posadas?
sources.supports: Mexican colonial context, observance from 16 to 24 December and competing origin explanations, including the Acolman 1587 account.
sources.limit: The article itself signals disagreement; 1587 is an attributed origin, not a settled first occurrence.

uncertainty: Exact first origin and path of diffusion remain disputed.
Specific local prayers, routes and host practices vary; no one form should be called universal.

editorial_en.description: In Mexico and other Latin American communities, Las Posadas is celebrated on the nine evenings from 16 to 24 December during Advent. The Mexican colonial tradition recalls Mary and Joseph seeking lodging; an Acolman origin in 1587 is reported but disputed.
editorial_en.meaning: The journey invites hospitality toward the Holy Family, Christ and neighbour.
editorial_en.how: A household or parish may join a local procession with images, songs asking for lodging, prayer and a gathering at a host home.
editorial_en.optional: A voluntary regional devotion where a community observes it; it is not a universal Advent practice or part of the 1962 Mass.
editorial_en.caution: Local forms differ. The date range is customary, not a required novena; no single origin account is settled.

editorial_fr.description: Au Mexique et dans d’autres communautés latino-américaines, Las Posadas se célèbre pendant les neuf soirées du 16 au 24 décembre, en Avent. Cette tradition catholique du Mexique colonial évoque la recherche d’un abri par Marie et Joseph ; l’origine à Acolman en 1587 est rapportée, mais contestée.
editorial_fr.meaning: La marche invite à accueillir la Sainte Famille, le Christ et le prochain.
editorial_fr.how: Une famille ou une paroisse peut se joindre à une procession locale avec des images, des chants demandant l’hospitalité, une prière et un rassemblement dans une maison d’accueil.
editorial_fr.optional: Dévotion régionale facultative là où une communauté la pratique ; ce n’est ni un usage universel de l’Avent ni une partie de la messe de 1962.
editorial_fr.caution: Les formes locales varient. Les neuf soirées sont une coutume, non une neuvaine obligatoire ; l’origine exacte n’est pas établie.

records.title_fr: Le partage de l’opłatek à la veille de Noël
records.geography: Especially Polish households and Polish communities abroad; related Christmas wafers exist in neighbouring Central and Eastern European traditions.
records.occasion: Christmas Eve (24 December), the vigil of the Nativity in the 1962 calendar.
records.history: A Polish Catholic household custom centred on a thin, unleavened, image-embossed Christmas wafer. The precise date of origin is not established by the consulted sources.
records.meaning: The family shares good wishes, peace and reconciliation while preparing for the celebration of Christ's Nativity.
records.practice: Before the Wigilia meal, family members break and share pieces of opłatek with one another and exchange wishes. It is a domestic wafer, not the Eucharist or Holy Communion.
records.contemporary: Appropriate as an optional family or community custom, including in diaspora households. Families may adapt or omit it without implying deficient observance.
records.liturgical_class: Regional domestic Christmas custom on the vigil; distinct from the liturgy and the Blessed Sacrament.
records.owner_reference: XMAS-001; existing Calendar/Customs Atlas owner. Do not create a duplicate Christmas Eve record.

sources.name: Culture.pl, Polish Christmas Eve Traditions
sources.supports: Current Polish family practice: religious-image wafer shared before supper with mutual good wishes; situates it within 24 December Wigilia.
sources.limit: Cultural overview; does not establish an exact medieval origin.

sources.name: Polish Bishops' Conference, Polish Christmas Traditions
sources.supports: The family reads Scripture about Christ's birth and shares the Christmas wafer with good wishes before the meal.
sources.limit: A present-day episcopal description, not a ritual directive or universal household norm.

uncertainty: Older-origin claims need archival corroboration; avoid a precise century.
Related wafers in Lithuania, Slovakia and elsewhere should retain their own names and local details.

editorial_en.description: Especially in Polish households, opłatek is shared before the Wigilia supper on Christmas Eve, 24 December, the vigil of the Nativity. It is a thin, image-embossed wafer; the sources confirm the custom but not a precise early date.
editorial_en.meaning: Sharing good wishes expresses peace, reconciliation and family fellowship before celebrating Christ's birth.
editorial_en.how: Family members break and share pieces of the wafer and exchange wishes before the meal.
editorial_en.optional: A voluntary Polish household custom, also practised in diaspora communities; families may adapt it.
editorial_en.caution: Opłatek is not the Eucharist or Holy Communion. Related regional Christmas wafers should retain their own names and traditions.

editorial_fr.description: Surtout dans les familles polonaises, l’opłatek se partage avant le repas de Wigilia, le 24 décembre, veille de la Nativité. Cette mince hostie non consacrée porte une image en relief ; les sources attestent la coutume sans en fixer précisément l’ancienneté.
editorial_fr.meaning: L’échange de vœux exprime la paix, le pardon et l’unité familiale avant la célébration de la naissance du Christ.
editorial_fr.how: Les membres de la famille rompent et partagent des morceaux de l’opłatek en se souhaitant mutuellement le bien avant le repas.
editorial_fr.optional: Coutume familiale polonaise facultative, également pratiquée dans les communautés de diaspora ; chaque famille peut l’adapter.
editorial_fr.caution: L’opłatek n’est pas l’Eucharistie ni la sainte communion. Les pains de Noël d’autres régions gardent leurs noms et leurs formes propres.

records.title_fr: Visiter les églises le Jeudi saint
records.geography: Roman Catholic practice with strong Roman associations and documented use in Latin America, Italy, Poland, the Philippines and other local communities.
records.occasion: After the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, during the Triduum.
records.history: Catholic sources connect the practice with Rome and the sixteenth-century pilgrimages popularised by St Philip Neri. The origins and local forms of Holy Thursday visits are not identical to Rome's separate pilgrimage to its seven basilicas.
records.meaning: The faithful keep watch with Christ and pray before the Eucharist at the altar of repose, recalling Gethsemane and the Passion.
records.practice: Where churches are open, a person or family may make one or several quiet visits, pray briefly and respect each parish's posted access and prayer arrangements. Seven stops are a customary form in some places, not a requirement.
records.contemporary: A voluntary devotion appropriate where safely and practically available. Never leave children unsupervised, presume a church is open, or displace participation in the parish liturgy.
records.liturgical_class: Popular Eucharistic devotion accompanying Holy Thursday; separate from the Mass and from the Church's official Triduum rites.
records.owner_reference: HTHU-001; existing Calendar/Customs Atlas owner. Annual date is calculated by Calendar; do not add a separate feast or itinerary.

sources.name: EWTN News, Why do Catholics visit 7 churches on Holy Thursday?
sources.supports: Current Holy Thursday visits to altars of repose, prayer on the Passion and a Roman/St Philip Neri history account.
sources.limit: A popular contemporary explanation; does not establish a universal number or obligation.

sources.name: Archdiocese of Sydney, Holy Thursday Visitation of the Seven Churches
sources.supports: Voluntary visits between churches, prayer before altars of repose and the association with St Philip Neri.
sources.limit: A local pastoral guide; follow local church access and liturgical arrangements.

uncertainty: Exact chronology between Rome's seven-basilica pilgrimage and dispersed Holy Thursday altar visits varies among accounts.
No indulgence, prescribed set of prayers or seven-visit obligation is asserted.

editorial_en.description: On Holy Thursday, after the Mass of the Lord's Supper, Catholics in many regions make voluntary visits to churches where the altar of repose is open. The practice has Roman associations and was popularised by St Philip Neri; local forms vary.
editorial_en.meaning: Prayer at the altar of repose recalls Christ in Gethsemane and keeps watch with Him before the Passion.
editorial_en.how: A person or family may visit one or several accessible churches and pray quietly, following local access and parish directions.
editorial_en.optional: A popular devotion distinct from the Triduum liturgy; seven visits are not required.
editorial_en.caution: Do not presume a church is open or treat a set number, route or prayer formula as universal.

editorial_fr.description: Le Jeudi saint, après la messe de la Cène du Seigneur, des fidèles de plusieurs régions visitent librement des églises où se trouve l’autel du repos. La pratique est associée à Rome et fut popularisée par saint Philippe Néri ; ses formes locales varient.
editorial_fr.meaning: La prière à l’autel du repos rappelle le Christ à Gethsémani et invite à veiller avec lui avant sa Passion.
editorial_fr.how: Une personne ou une famille peut visiter une ou plusieurs églises accessibles et prier en silence, selon les consignes paroissiales.
editorial_fr.optional: Dévotion populaire distincte de la liturgie du Triduum ; les sept visites ne sont pas obligatoires.
editorial_fr.caution: Ne pas présumer qu’une église est ouverte ni présenter un nombre, un itinéraire ou une formule de prière comme universels.

records.title_fr: La couronne de l’Avent en famille
records.geography: Originated in nineteenth-century Protestant Hamburg; adopted and adapted by Catholic families and parishes in Germany and later elsewhere.
records.occasion: The Sundays of Advent; the first Sunday is determined by the 1962 calendar.
records.history: The Cologne Archdiocese traces the original Wichern wreath to 1839, with four candles becoming the common form and wider Catholic adoption in Germany occurring chiefly after the Second World War. This is a Christian custom received into Catholic home devotion, not an ancient Roman rite.
records.meaning: Increasing candlelight marks expectation of Christ's Nativity; evergreen boughs can signify life and hope.
records.practice: A household may light one additional candle on each Advent Sunday and pray, sing or read Scripture together. Any blessing belongs to an authorised minister using an applicable rite; families need not seek one to use a wreath.
records.contemporary: Widely suitable as optional family prayer. Candle colours and exact weekly forms vary; they do not determine Mass vestments or create obligations.
records.liturgical_class: Household Advent devotion, distinct from the 1962 Mass and its official propers.
records.owner_reference: ADVT-001; existing Calendar/Customs Atlas owner. Calendar supplies Advent Sundays.

sources.name: Archdiocese of Cologne, Der Adventskranz: Bedeutung und Ursprung
sources.supports: Wichern's original wheel with 23 candles, evolution to four candles, spread into Catholic churches in Cologne and broader Germany.
sources.limit: Regional diocesan history; local dates for first adoption are reported as such.

sources.name: Vatican State, winter issue on Christmas traditions
sources.supports: Places the wreath's origin in nineteenth-century Germany and describes later spread to neighbouring countries.
sources.limit: General historical overview; does not turn household use into liturgical law.

sources.name: USCCB, Blessing of an Advent Wreath
sources.supports: A current Catholic family setting for Advent wreath prayer and a separate published blessing resource.
sources.limit: A blessing text is not evidence that a priest must bless every wreath or that families may perform a priestly blessing.

uncertainty: Chronology and first Catholic domestic use differ among secondary summaries; 1925 Cologne refers to a Catholic church wreath, not the first household wreath.

editorial_en.description: The Advent wreath began in nineteenth-century Germany in a Protestant setting and was later adopted in Catholic homes and churches. Families commonly light candles on the Sundays of Advent, whose dates are set by the 1962 calendar.
editorial_en.meaning: Growing candlelight points toward Christ's coming; evergreen branches can suggest life and hope.
editorial_en.how: A household may light one additional candle each Advent Sunday and pray or sing together.
editorial_en.optional: A widely used but optional household devotion, separate from the 1962 Mass and its propers.
editorial_en.caution: Candle colours and home customs vary. A ministerial blessing, if desired, is separate from family prayer.

editorial_fr.description: La couronne de l’Avent apparaît dans l’Allemagne du XIXe siècle, dans un contexte protestant, avant d’être reçue dans les foyers et les églises catholiques. Les familles allument généralement les cierges les dimanches de l’Avent, déterminés par le calendrier de 1962.
editorial_fr.meaning: La lumière croissante annonce la venue du Christ ; les branches persistantes peuvent évoquer la vie et l’espérance.
editorial_fr.how: Une famille peut allumer un cierge supplémentaire chaque dimanche de l’Avent et prier ou chanter ensemble.
editorial_fr.optional: Dévotion domestique répandue mais facultative, distincte de la messe de 1962 et de ses propres.
editorial_fr.caution: Les couleurs des cierges et les usages domestiques varient. Une bénédiction ministérielle éventuelle reste distincte de la prière familiale.

records.title_fr: Une marche de prière familiale aux Rogations
records.geography: A contemporary household adaptation of the wider Western Catholic Rogation tradition; no single national household form established.
records.occasion: A Rogation day: Major Rogation on 25 April, or the Minor Rogation days before Ascension, as calculated by the 1962 Calendar.
records.history: Historical Rogation processions were public ecclesiastical processions with prayers for the land and its produce. Recent Catholic family accounts document a household walk as a practical domestic adaptation; that does not prove it was a universal or inherited historical family custom.
records.meaning: Prayer expresses dependence on God, gratitude for creation and concern for crops, work, animals and neighbours.
records.practice: A family may take a short walk around a garden, allotment or safe nearby route, pray for farmers and workers, and give thanks for the earth's fruits. It need not imitate a parish procession or use holy water.
records.contemporary: Suitable as a voluntary family prayer practice, including for households without farmland. Keep it distinct from ministerial field blessings and from the official Rogation liturgy.
records.liturgical_class: Historic Rogation observances are liturgical/processional; this household walk is an optional contemporary adaptation.
records.owner_reference: ROGA-001; existing Calendar/Customs Atlas owner. Calendar alone supplies the annually correct Rogation dates.

sources.name: Catholic Culture, A Family Rogation Walk
sources.supports: A Catholic family guide proposing a walk and prayer for gardens and fields.
sources.limit: Modern devotional guidance; not proof of a centuries-old household custom.

sources.name: National Catholic Register, When Rogation Days Filled Our Yard With Prayer, Processions and Shortcake
sources.supports: First-person contemporary family practice of walking around property while praying for a fruitful harvest.
sources.limit: Personal household witness; not a normative rite or broad historical survey.

sources.name: Catholic Encyclopedia, Processions
sources.supports: Historical Rogation processions, prayer for the earth's produce, parish-boundary perambulation and clergy-led practice.
sources.limit: Historical ecclesiastical processions are evidence for the broader observance, not for the household adaptation.

uncertainty: Independent historical evidence for this exact domestic form is limited; retain 'optional contemporary adaptation'.
Do not supply a lay ritual, field-sprinkling formula or claim that a priestly blessing is available.

editorial_en.description: The 1962 calendar marks Major Rogation on 25 April and Minor Rogation days before Ascension. Historic public processions are well attested; a family walk is better described as a contemporary household adaptation.
editorial_en.meaning: Prayer gives thanks for creation and asks God's care for land, work, crops, animals and neighbours.
editorial_en.how: A family may take a short safe walk near a garden or home and pray for farmers and workers, without imitating a clerical procession.
editorial_en.optional: An optional family prayer practice; no farmland, holy water or special ceremony is required.
editorial_en.caution: Keep this separate from a priest's procession or field blessing. Evidence for an old universal household form is lacking.

editorial_fr.description: Le calendrier de 1962 marque les Rogations majeures le 25 avril et les Rogations mineures avant l’Ascension. Les processions publiques anciennes sont bien attestées ; la marche en famille se décrit plus justement comme une adaptation domestique contemporaine.
editorial_fr.meaning: La prière rend grâce pour la création et demande à Dieu de veiller sur la terre, le travail, les récoltes, les animaux et le prochain.
editorial_fr.how: Une famille peut faire une courte promenade sûre près de son jardin ou de son foyer et prier pour les agriculteurs et les travailleurs, sans imiter une procession cléricale.
editorial_fr.optional: Pratique de prière familiale facultative ; ni terre agricole, ni eau bénite, ni cérémonie particulière ne sont nécessaires.
editorial_fr.caution: La distinguer d’une procession ou d’une bénédiction des champs présidée par un prêtre. Une ancienne coutume familiale universelle n’est pas établie.

records.title_en: The Advent manger of good deeds
records.title_fr: La crèche préparée par les bonnes actions
records.geography: A family devotion described as French in a modern Catholic family account; an independent historical French origin has not been verified.
records.occasion: During Advent, with the manger completed before or at Christmas.
records.history: The reviewed independent witness is a contemporary Catholic family's account that labels the activity French. It documents present devotional use, not the date or geographic origin of the practice.
records.meaning: Children connect kindness, prayer and preparation of the heart with welcoming the Christ Child.
records.practice: A household may place a piece of straw or paper in an empty manger after a child's act of kindness or prayer, gradually preparing a place for a Nativity figure.
records.contemporary: A simple optional family devotion if used without pressure, competition or reward accounting. The published regional-origin attribution remains explicitly uncertain.
records.liturgical_class: Household Advent devotion; not a 1962 liturgical action, indulgenced practice or required preparation.
records.owner_reference: ADVT-002; existing Calendar/Customs Atlas owner. Preserve its current bounded scope and source caveat.

sources.name: Catholic Culture, Straws in the Manger—Preparing Our Hearts for Christ's Birth
sources.supports: A contemporary Catholic family report calls it a French custom and describes adding straw for children's kindness, obedience, help and prayer.
sources.limit: One modern family account; does not independently verify French historical origin or prevalence.

sources.name: Polish Bishops' Conference, Polish Christmas Traditions
sources.supports: A separate Polish Christmas Eve practice places hay under the table as a reminder of the stable.
sources.limit: This is a different custom and does not corroborate straw placed in a manger in response to good deeds.

uncertainty: French origin and antiquity remain unverified independently; label as a modern family-reported custom, not a proven French historical tradition.
Do not conflate the Polish hay-under-table custom with the manger-straw practice.

editorial_en.description: A contemporary Catholic family account describes adding straw to an Advent manger after acts of kindness or prayer and calls the practice French. Independent evidence does not verify that historical origin.
editorial_en.meaning: Simple acts of charity help children prepare their hearts to welcome the Christ Child.
editorial_en.how: A family may place a small piece of straw or paper in an empty manger after a child's kindness, help or prayer.
editorial_en.optional: A voluntary family devotion without scoring or pressure, completed before or at Christmas.
editorial_en.caution: Present the French attribution as unverified; do not conflate this with hay placed under a Polish Christmas Eve table.

editorial_fr.description: Un témoignage familial catholique contemporain décrit l’ajout de paille dans une crèche de l’Avent après des actes de bonté ou une prière, et qualifie l’usage de français. Les sources indépendantes ne confirment pas cette origine historique.
editorial_fr.meaning: De simples actes de charité aident les enfants à préparer leur cœur à accueillir l’Enfant Jésus.
editorial_fr.how: Une famille peut déposer un brin de paille ou un morceau de papier dans une crèche vide après un geste de bonté, un service ou une prière de l’enfant.
editorial_fr.optional: Dévotion familiale facultative, sans points ni pression, achevée avant ou à Noël.
editorial_fr.caution: Présenter l’attribution française comme incertaine ; ne pas confondre cet usage avec le foin placé sous la table polonaise de la veille de Noël.

records.title_fr: Les chanteurs de l’Étoile à l’Épiphanie (Sternsinger)
records.geography: Austria and German-speaking Catholic regions, with distinct local forms.
records.occasion: Around Epiphany (6 January in the 1962 Roman calendar); local visits may take place on nearby days.
records.history: The Austrian Catholic Jungschar's Three Kings Action describes a medieval practice of costumed singers visiting homes and a modern charitable revival in Austria beginning in 1954. Its modern campaign is not the whole historical custom.
records.meaning: Children recall the Magi's homage to Christ and express Christian charity by bringing greetings and raising support for people in need.
records.practice: Children or parish groups dress as the Magi, carry a star, sing or offer a greeting at homes, and may collect donations for organised charity. Door-lintel writing or stickers are a related local practice and should not be presented as a lay sacramental blessing formula.
records.contemporary: A living optional parish/community tradition where organised; charity collection depends on a real, accountable campaign. No household is obliged to receive singers or give money.
records.liturgical_class: Regional Epiphany popular custom and charitable campaign, separate from Epiphany Mass and priestly house blessings.
records.owner_reference: Potential Customs Atlas candidate; existing Epiphany Calendar context can link only to an actual locally organised event. No second Epiphany feast or invented map pin.

sources.name: Dreikönigsaktion der Katholischen Jungschar, Hintergründe zum Sternsingen
sources.supports: Austrian Catholic organisation describes house-to-house song, greetings, charitable fundraising, medieval roots and its 1954 revival.
sources.limit: Institutional history is about the Austrian tradition and campaign, not every German regional variant.

sources.name: Archdiocese of Cologne, Heilige Drei Könige: Herkunft und Bedeutung des Feiertags
sources.supports: German children dressed as the Magi visit homes around 6 January, offer a blessing greeting and raise support for children in need.
sources.limit: Current German practice; the wording C+M+B is not in itself a priestly blessing.

uncertainty: Exact medieval origins and continuity vary by locality; the secure, documented Austrian charitable revival begins in 1954.

editorial_en.description: Around Epiphany, children dressed as the Magi visit homes in Austrian and German Catholic communities, bringing greetings and, in organised campaigns, collecting for charity. The Austrian Catholic youth organisation describes medieval antecedents and a charitable revival in 1954.
editorial_en.meaning: The custom recalls the Magi's homage to Christ and turns the Christmas message toward service of people in need.
editorial_en.how: Children or parish groups may carry a star, sing or offer a greeting, and take part in an accountable local charity campaign.
editorial_en.optional: A regional parish custom around 6 January, not an Epiphany Mass rite or household obligation.
editorial_en.caution: Do not equate door lettering with a priestly house blessing or presume a donation is required.

editorial_fr.description: Autour de l’Épiphanie, des enfants vêtus en Mages visitent des maisons dans les communautés catholiques d’Autriche et d’Allemagne, transmettent des vœux et, dans les campagnes organisées, recueillent des fonds pour des œuvres. L’organisation catholique autrichienne décrit des antécédents médiévaux et une relance caritative en 1954.
editorial_fr.meaning: La coutume rappelle l’hommage des Mages au Christ et prolonge le message de Noël par le service des personnes dans le besoin.
editorial_fr.how: Les enfants ou groupes paroissiaux peuvent porter une étoile, chanter ou saluer les habitants et participer à une campagne caritative locale transparente.
editorial_fr.optional: Coutume paroissiale régionale autour du 6 janvier, distincte de la messe de l’Épiphanie et sans obligation pour les foyers.
editorial_fr.caution: Ne pas assimiler l’inscription sur une porte à une bénédiction sacerdotale du foyer ni imposer un don.

records.title_en: French Epiphany cake and the share for a guest or poor person
records.title_fr: La galette des Rois et la part de l’hôte ou du pauvre
records.geography: France, with regional distinction between northern frangipane galette and southern brioche/couronne des rois; similar cakes elsewhere are not identical.
records.occasion: Epiphany; 6 January in the 1962 calendar. The family custom may be observed on a nearby Sunday or gathering date.
records.history: The French Bishops' Conference describes the galette custom as attested from the fourteenth century and distinguishes regional forms. Its account also repeats pre-Christian and Roman explanations; these should be labelled as traditional theories, not settled origin.
records.meaning: The shared cake makes a family celebration of the Magi and can express hospitality. The Gospel celebration is liturgical; cake and bean are customary domestic additions.
records.practice: A household shares a galette or regional king cake, often with a hidden bean or fève to name a festive king or queen. The French Bishops' Conference says some households keep an extra portion for a poor person or stranger; this is optional and locally variable.
records.contemporary: Appropriate as optional seasonal food and hospitality. Do not claim the cake is a Catholic sacramental, required on the feast, or a payment for education.
records.liturgical_class: French regional household food custom associated with Epiphany; not a universal Catholic observance.
records.owner_reference: Provisional owner: French Epiphany Calendar/household content. Reconcile with existing Epiphany card; avoid separate feast identity or a universal poor-share instruction.

sources.name: Conférence des évêques de France, Fête de l'Épiphanie en Occident, la « fête des Rois »
sources.supports: French regional galette and brioche distinctions, fourteenth-century attestation, and an optional extra share for the poor or stranger.
sources.limit: The article repeats older origin theories; its evidence supports the custom, not every explanation for its origin.

sources.name: French Ministry of Agriculture, Après les fêtes... place à la galette !
sources.supports: The king cake is traditionally consumed at Epiphany and traces the French history of the cake.
sources.limit: Food-history overview; not a liturgical source.

sources.name: Institut de France, Le gâteau ou la galette des Rois
sources.supports: Sixteenth-century culinary sources describe drawing the bean and reserving a portion for God/poor.
sources.limit: The Saturnalia connection is expressed as a possibility, not proof of direct continuity.

uncertainty: Direct descent from Roman Saturnalia is unproven; keep only as a commonly repeated theory if mentioned.
The extra poor-person's share is historically attested in some accounts but not universal today.
A 1962 feast date and a modern French Sunday celebration should not be conflated.

editorial_en.description: In France, Epiphany sharing may use a northern frangipane galette or a southern brioche cake. Church and cultural sources attest the custom by the fourteenth century and say some households reserve an extra portion for a poor person or stranger; origin theories remain uncertain.
editorial_en.meaning: The shared cake marks a festive family gathering for Epiphany and can express hospitality.
editorial_en.how: A household shares a cake, often with a hidden bean or fève; in some accounts an extra piece is set aside for a poor person or guest.
editorial_en.optional: An optional regional food custom associated with Epiphany, not a sacramental or required observance.
editorial_en.caution: Do not teach direct descent from Roman Saturnalia as fact, or imply that every family makes a poor person's share.

editorial_fr.description: En France, le partage à l’Épiphanie peut se faire autour d’une galette à la frangipane au nord ou d’une brioche au sud. Des sources ecclésiales et culturelles attestent l’usage dès le XIVe siècle ; certaines familles réservent une part au pauvre ou à l’étranger, mais les théories sur l’origine restent incertaines.
editorial_fr.meaning: Le gâteau partagé accompagne la fête familiale de l’Épiphanie et peut exprimer l’hospitalité.
editorial_fr.how: La famille partage un gâteau, souvent avec une fève cachée ; certains témoignages mentionnent une part supplémentaire destinée à un pauvre ou à un hôte.
editorial_fr.optional: Coutume alimentaire régionale facultative associée à l’Épiphanie, ni sacramentelle ni obligatoire.
editorial_fr.caution: Ne pas présenter comme un fait une filiation directe avec les Saturnales romaines ni affirmer que chaque famille réserve une part au pauvre.

canonical_owner.owner: Potential regional Customs Atlas entry; related but distinct facets are carpets and decorated windows/routes

records.title_en: Flowers and carpets along Corpus Christi routes
records.title_fr: Fleurs et tapis sur les parcours de la Fête-Dieu
records.geography: Documented local forms include Arbúcies in Catalonia and Ponteareas in Galicia; other European localities have their own histories and designs.
records.occasion: The Corpus Christi feast and its actual local procession. The 1962 calendar places Corpus Christi on Thursday after Trinity Sunday; local civil processions may be arranged differently.
records.history: Catalonia's heritage authority documents Arbúcies Enramades from at least the sixteenth century; flower carpets along the Blessed Sacrament procession route remain part of the local custom. Galicia's tourism authority describes a separate Ponteareas carpet practice of more than 150 years.
records.meaning: Flowers and temporary artwork are offerings of honour to the Eucharistic procession and expressions of local participation.
records.practice: Residents, families and parish groups may gather flowers and lay temporary carpets or decorate windows and streets where this is an established local practice and a procession is actually scheduled.
records.contemporary: A living regional custom in named communities. Do not infer it for every parish, attach a procession to the feast date, or merge carpets, window adornment and distinct local art forms into one universal practice.
records.liturgical_class: Regional public popular custom associated with a liturgical feast; decoration itself is neither liturgical obligation nor official blessing.
records.owner_reference: Provisional regional Customs Atlas candidate. Retain geographic facets; link Calendar only to verified local events. No automatic route/map pins.

sources.name: Catalan Government Heritage, Arbúcies Festival of Enramades
sources.supports: Sixteenth-century documentary mention, women and children gathering flowers, carpets along Corpus Christi processional route, and later change in the procession's role.
sources.limit: Evidence is specific to Arbúcies; later secular festival elements are distinguished from the earlier Blessed Sacrament procession.

sources.name: Galicia Tourism, Festivals of International Tourist Interest: Corpus Christi, Ponteareas
sources.supports: More-than-150-year local flower carpets, made by residents overnight as offerings along a Corpus Christi procession route.
sources.limit: Official tourism description of a particular local celebration; calendar placement and procession schedule are local.

uncertainty: The precise earliest origin is unclear for these crafts and differs by place.
Arbúcies' current secular festival is not identical to the earlier procession custom.
Local feast/procession transfer must be verified; calendar date alone does not establish an event.

editorial_en.description: Local Corpus Christi customs include flower carpets along processional routes in Arbúcies, Catalonia, documented from the sixteenth century, and in Ponteareas, Galicia, where a separate practice is more than 150 years old. Other towns have distinct forms.
editorial_en.meaning: Residents offer temporary floral art in honour of the Blessed Sacrament and participate in local public devotion.
editorial_en.how: Where customary and locally announced, families and neighbours may gather flowers and decorate streets, windows or a route before the procession.
editorial_en.optional: A regional community custom, not a decoration required of every parish; the actual local procession date must be checked.
editorial_en.caution: The 1962 feast date does not establish a route or event. Preserve each locality and distinguish carpets from window decoration.

editorial_fr.description: Les usages locaux de la Fête-Dieu comprennent les tapis de fleurs le long du parcours à Arbúcies, en Catalogne, attestés depuis le XVIe siècle, et à Ponteareas, en Galice, où une pratique distincte existe depuis plus de 150 ans. D’autres villes ont leurs propres formes.
editorial_fr.meaning: Les habitants offrent une œuvre florale éphémère en l’honneur du Saint-Sacrement et prennent part à la dévotion publique locale.
editorial_fr.how: Là où l’usage existe et où une procession est annoncée, les familles et voisins peuvent cueillir des fleurs et décorer la rue, les fenêtres ou le parcours.
editorial_fr.optional: Coutume communautaire régionale, sans décoration imposée à chaque paroisse ; il faut vérifier la date de la procession locale.
editorial_fr.caution: La date de la fête selon le calendrier de 1962 ne crée ni parcours ni événement. Préserver les spécificités locales et distinguer les tapis des fenêtres ornées.

canonical_owner.owner: Easter-season household or parish Calendar/Customs Atlas content

records.title_fr: La marche d’Emmaüs du lundi de Pâques
records.geography: Documented especially in southern Germany and Austrian parishes; local forms differ.
records.occasion: Easter Monday, the Monday within the Easter Octave in the 1962 calendar.
records.history: The Diocese of Essen defines the Emmausgang as a living southern German custom; Vatican News reports it as an Easter Monday practice in many Austrian parishes. It is an Easter devotion inspired by Luke 24:13–35, not a required liturgical procession.
records.meaning: Walking recalls the disciples' encounter with the risen Christ and the recognition of Jesus in the breaking of bread.
records.practice: A parish or family may take a reflective walk with prayer or song, sometimes ending with Mass outdoors where organised. A quiet family walk may keep the Gospel story in view without claiming to reproduce an official ceremony.
records.contemporary: Appropriate as an optional Easter devotion. Some places now treat it mainly as a spring outing; regional vitality and religious character vary.
records.liturgical_class: Regional Easter popular custom on Easter Monday, separate from the Mass and from the proper of the day.
records.owner_reference: Provisional Easter-season Calendar/Customs Atlas content; avoid treating it as a fixed event without a local source.

sources.name: Diocese of Essen, Emmausgang
sources.supports: A living southern German Easter Monday custom of a prayerful walk with song or a contemplative Easter walk, tied to Luke 24.
sources.limit: The diocese notes many contemporary walks are understood mainly as spring walks.

sources.name: Vatican News, Stichwort: Ostermontag
sources.supports: The Emmaus narrative's place in Easter Monday and parish Emmausgangs with prayer, song and sometimes an outdoor Mass in Austria.
sources.limit: Current Austrian witness; outdoor Mass depends on an actual parish celebration.

uncertainty: Exact historical beginnings of the modern walk are not established by these sources.
Weiser's French/Canadian grandparent-visiting variant is not verified by these witnesses and must not be folded into the German/Austrian practice.

editorial_en.description: In southern Germany and Austrian parishes, the Emmausgang takes place on Easter Monday, with prayer and song or as a reflective spring walk. It recalls Luke's account of the disciples meeting the risen Christ on the road to Emmaus.
editorial_en.meaning: The walk turns attention to the risen Christ, Scripture and recognition of the Lord in the breaking of bread.
editorial_en.how: A family may take a quiet walk and recall Luke 24; an organised parish outing or outdoor Mass should be joined only when actually scheduled.
editorial_en.optional: A regional Easter custom, not a required procession or substitute for the day's liturgy; some places now treat it mainly as a spring outing.
editorial_en.caution: The French and Canadian family-visiting variant reported by Weiser was not confirmed by the sources reviewed.

editorial_fr.description: Dans le sud de l’Allemagne et des paroisses autrichiennes, l’Emmausgang a lieu le lundi de Pâques : marche de réflexion accompagnée de prière et de chants, ou promenade printanière. Il rappelle le récit de Luc où les disciples rencontrent le Christ ressuscité sur le chemin d’Emmaüs.
editorial_fr.meaning: La marche tourne le regard vers le Christ ressuscité, l’Écriture et la reconnaissance du Seigneur à la fraction du pain.
editorial_fr.how: Une famille peut se promener en méditant Luc 24 ; une sortie paroissiale ou une messe en plein air ne se rejoint que si elle est effectivement organisée.
editorial_fr.optional: Coutume pascale régionale, sans procession obligatoire et sans remplacement de la liturgie ; certains lieux la vivent aujourd’hui surtout comme une promenade printanière.
editorial_fr.caution: La variante française et canadienne de visite aux grands-parents mentionnée par Weiser n’a pas été confirmée par les sources consultées.

canonical_owner.owner: Potential household Marian devotion; cross-reference DEV-001 May as the month of Mary without claiming identity

records.title_en: A small garden dedicated to Our Lady
records.title_fr: Un petit jardin dédié à Notre-Dame
records.geography: Documented modern Catholic household and parish practice in the United States, inspired by older European Marian flower names; individual gardens are local.
records.occasion: Spring, May, or any suitable growing season; no fixed feast date.
records.history: The University of Dayton Marian Library documents a public Mary Garden at Woods Hole, Massachusetts, established in 1932, and a 1951 Philadelphia initiative that encouraged household gardens. Medieval Marian plant names are an older strand of flower symbolism, but they do not prove that today's Mary Garden form is medieval.
records.meaning: A tended garden can prompt prayer, gratitude for creation and reflection on Mary's place in the life of Christ.
records.practice: A household may plant locally suitable flowers or herbs and use them as reminders for a short Marian prayer. Traditional flower names are optional and should be described as folklore where their history is uncertain.
records.contemporary: Suitable as a voluntary low-cost or no-cost devotion; even a pot or an existing garden corner is enough. No plant has magical or medicinal power by virtue of a Marian name.
records.liturgical_class: Domestic Marian devotion, not a liturgical observance, sacramental or required May practice.
records.owner_reference: Potential distinct household custom; cross-link DEV-001 only as related Marian devotion. Avoid duplicate May devotion or a new Calendar feast.

sources.name: University of Dayton Marian Library, Background on Mary's Gardens
sources.supports: Public Woods Hole garden in 1932; 1951 Philadelphia organization promoting home gardens as a religious work of stewardship and devotion.
sources.limit: Institutional archive/history supports the modern movement, not an ancient universal garden custom.

sources.name: University of Dayton, 'Mary gardens' bring Catholic piety to the garden
sources.supports: Modern Marian garden practice and the historical interest in traditional plant names.
sources.limit: The article explicitly notes inconsistencies in folk names and associated legends.

sources.name: Howth Parish, The Mary Garden at Our Lady of the Assumption
sources.supports: A contemporary Irish parish garden used as a place of beauty, reflection and prayer.
sources.limit: A local example, not evidence of Irish or universal historical origin.

uncertainty: Do not project the 1930s–1950s named Mary Garden movement into medieval history.
Plant legends vary and should never be asserted as fact without separate historical evidence.

editorial_en.description: The modern Catholic Mary Garden movement is documented in the United States from a public garden at Woods Hole in 1932 and a home-garden initiative in 1951. It draws on older Marian flower names, but the present garden form is not thereby proven medieval.
editorial_en.meaning: Caring for plants can prompt gratitude for creation and prayerful reflection on Mary and the life of Christ.
editorial_en.how: A household may tend a few suitable flowers or herbs, even in pots, and use them as reminders for a short Marian prayer.
editorial_en.optional: A flexible household devotion for spring, May or another growing season, with no required plant or purchase.
editorial_en.caution: Flower names and legends differ; do not state folklore as history or attribute magical or medicinal effects to a plant.

editorial_fr.description: Le mouvement catholique moderne des jardins marials est attesté aux États-Unis par un jardin public à Woods Hole en 1932 et une initiative de jardins domestiques en 1951. Il s’inspire d’anciens noms de fleurs associés à Marie, sans que la forme actuelle du jardin soit pour autant prouvée médiévale.
editorial_fr.meaning: Le soin des plantes peut éveiller la gratitude pour la création et la prière contemplative à propos de Marie et de la vie du Christ.
editorial_fr.how: Une famille peut cultiver quelques fleurs ou herbes adaptées, même en pots, et s’en servir comme rappel pour une brève prière mariale.
editorial_fr.optional: Dévotion domestique souple au printemps, en mai ou durant une autre saison de jardinage, sans plante ni achat obligatoire.
editorial_fr.caution: Les noms et légendes florales varient ; ne pas présenter le folklore comme histoire ni prêter aux plantes des effets magiques ou médicinaux.
